SMART idea 2 – Let’s take a vote! (concept checking)

 Time required: 10–15 minutes
 Materials required:

       • Voting cards (supplied below) or ask students to make their own voting cards
      • Planned concept check questions
 Learning objec�ve:
       • To check understanding of a language item or grammatical structure
       • To take a ‘snapshot’ of learners’ understanding using the voting cards
      • The example given below concept checks the second conditional, but the voting

           cards can be used to concept check other language points

Write a sentence on the board which includes the target structure you want to check, for
example:

       If I won the lottery I would buy a sports car

Distribute a set of voting cards to each of the learners: Yes / No / Don’t know / Real /
Imaginary
Option: Ask learners to make their own cards on different pieces of paper in large letters
(that you will be able to see from the front of the class).

Concept check ques�ons (for the example sentence and structure)
    1. Have I won the lottery?
    2. Am I going to win the lottery?
    3. Am I going to get a car?

    4. Have I bought a lottery ticket?
    5. Is this real or imaginary?

Steps for checking the concept

    1. Ask each concept check question one at a time.
    2. Ask learners to hold up their voting card after each question.
    3. Look around the class to check how learners have voted.
    4. Do learners understand the concept you are checking?
    5. Ask learners to explain their choices to give you more information about how they

         understand the concept.

Top �ps for wri�ng concept check ques�ons

    1. Always prepare your questions before the lesson.
    2. Check you understand the target structure.
    3. Questions should be easy to understand – aim them just below the learners’ language level.
    4. Use yes / no questions.
    5. Ask simple Wh- questions.
    6. Never include the target structure.
    7. Never use unfamiliar vocabulary.
Second condi�onal language notes
    • We use the second conditional when we imagine a situation in the present or future that is

         unreal, unlikely, or impossible.
    • The unreal situation is presented in the ‘if’ clause (if + past simple).
    • The result of the unreal situation is presented in the main clause (would + infinitive).
